title: Neat npm modules - Vol 1
content:
Document: WM-037                                                 P. Webb
Category: Review                                              2019.01.02

                        Neat npm modules - Vol 1

Abstract

   The modules you wish you used

Body

   This is the first post in what will become a series of posts about
   interesting and useful npm modules I come across and/or use in
   my projects.

   Over the past year, small modules that got to the point and had close
   to zero dependencies (dependency-free is even better!) became more
   appealing to me for a couple reasons.

   1. Big modules are slow to update. When a vulnerability is found in
      one of their dependencies the module maintainers are notified and
      then…nothing. Sometimes the maintainers never respond so someone
      forks the project, updates the dependencies, and pushes that
      project under a new name. When security issues are discovered, I
      want them resolved ASAP. Smaller modules have less attack area,
      obviously. Fewer moving parts, &c.
   2. The left-pad incident<a href="https://blog.npmjs.org/post/141577284765/kik-left-pad-and-npm?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[1]</a> and similarly befuddling things happening
      in the npm ecosphere give me pause about relying on a module with
      a bajillion moving parts. TL;DR: A popular module used by
      <em>thousands</em> of other modules was unpublished (removed) from npm
      and that caused QUITE the fuss when routine <code>npm install</code>s went
      off the rails across the Internet.

   Please note that <code>package.json</code> examples below only have the
   necessary parameters regarding the section its in. This is for
   brevity. New developers come into being every day I’d like to help
   them out by removing possible confusion.

   1. colorette

<blockquote>
   Colorette is a Node.js library for colorizing text in terminals.

</blockquote>

      Most people just use chalk<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/chalk?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[2]</a> to style terminal text and I did
      too. When I saw I could get the same functionality in a smaller
      dependency-free package, I jumped at the chance to use it. chalk
      does and supports a lot more but for <em>my</em> needs, colorette is
      juuuuust fine.

      Find it on npm<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/colorette?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[3]</a> | GitHub<a href="https://github.com/jorgebucaran/colorette?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[4]</a>

   2. husky

<blockquote>
   Husky can prevent bad git commit, git push and more 🐶 woof!

</blockquote>

      I’m honestly <em>embarrassed</em> that I haven’t used something like
      husky earlier in life. Husky saves you from <em>yourself</em> and what a
      beautiful job it does. Here’s how I use it in my <code>package.json</code>:

      <pre><code data-language="json">
      &quot;husky&quot;: {
        &quot;hooks&quot;: {
          &quot;pre-commit&quot;: &quot;npm run format &amp;&amp; npm run test:sass &amp;&amp; git add -A :/&quot;
        }
      },
      &quot;scripts&quot;: {
        &quot;format&quot;: &quot;eslint '*/*.js' --fix --ignore-pattern '/app/dist/'&quot;,
        &quot;test:sass&quot;: &quot;sass-lint --config ./node_modules/@inc/sasslint-config/config.json --verbose --no-exit&quot;
      }

</code></pre>

      What my pre-commit hook does is:

      1. Use eslint to automatically format issues in JavaScript files
         found in the codebase, except for JavaScript files in the
         folder <code>/app/dist/</code>.
      2. Use sass-lint and a custom configuration file to find issues in
         Sass files found in the codebase.
      3. Stage (prepare) the changed files, if any, to be committed to
         my git server (I self-host with Gitea but this works with any
         git server).

      Find it on npm<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/husky?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[5]</a> | GitHub<a href="https://github.com/typicode/husky?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[6]</a>

   3. npm-run-all

<blockquote>
   A CLI tool to run multiple npm-scripts in parallel
   or sequential.

</blockquote>

      Here’s how I use it in my <code>package.json</code>:

      <pre><code data-language="json">
      &quot;scripts&quot;: {
        &quot;test&quot;: &quot;run-s test:*&quot;,
        &quot;test:dependencies&quot;: &quot;updates --update ./ --exclude fastify&quot;,
        &quot;test:lint&quot;: &quot;standardx --verbose | snazzy&quot;,
        &quot;test:sass&quot;: &quot;sass-lint --config ./node_modules/@inc/sasslint-config/config.json --verbose --no-exit&quot;,
        &quot;watch&quot;: &quot;run-p watch:*&quot;,
        &quot;watch:sass&quot;: &quot;sass --watch app/sass:app/dist --style compressed&quot;,
        &quot;watch:server&quot;: &quot;NODE_ENV=development nodemon server&quot;
      }

</code></pre>

      <code>run-s</code> runs scripts sequentially, whereas <code>run-p</code> runs scripts in
      parallel. You’ve probably guessed by now but <code>run-s test:*</code> tells
      npm-run-all to run any script with "test:", one after the other.
      <code>run-p watch:*</code> tells it run any script with "watch:", side by
      side. I like it a lot.

      Find it on npm<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/npm-run-all?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[7]</a> | GitHub<a href="https://github.com/mysticatea/npm-run-all?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[8]</a>

   4. updates

<blockquote>
   Fast npm dependency updating tool

</blockquote>

      I found updates after being frustrated with npm-check-updates<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/npm-check-updates?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[9]</a>.
      One of the maintainers of the latter was uninterested<a href="https://github.com/tjunnone/npm-check-updates/issues/432?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[10]</a> in
      updating the dependencies. Forking and working on
      npm-check-updates myself proved to be annoying so I went looking
      for solutions elsewhere.

      Here’s how I use it in my <code>package.json</code> (fastify is working on
      their next version and it’s messing with this script so I ignore
      updating it for now):

      <pre><code data-language="json">
      &quot;scripts&quot;: {
        &quot;test:dependencies&quot;: &quot;updates --update ./ --exclude fastify&quot;
      }

</code></pre>

      Find it on npm<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/updates?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[11]</a> | GitHub<a href="https://github.com/silverwind/updates?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[12]</a>

   5. ver

<blockquote>
   Increment semantic versions across your project. Intended for
   projects with a package.json, but works with other files too.
   Will create a git commit and tag by default. By default, only
   the nearest package.json file is modified.

</blockquote>

      Before ver, I never cared about "semantic versioning", let alone
      versioning <em>itself</em>. ver makes it super low effort to do. I just
      run <code>ver patch|minor|major</code> and chain it with other commands. It
      will automatically update the "version" field in your
      <code>package.json</code> file. Pretty sweet.

      My typical usage is something like:

      <pre><code data-language="bash">
      ver patch &amp;&amp; git push &amp;&amp; npm publish

</code></pre>

      Find it on npm<a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/ver?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[13]</a> | GitHub<a href="https://github.com/silverwind/ver?ref=blog.webb.page" target="_blank">[14]</a>

   FIN

      And there you have it! Five neat modules I find incredibly useful.
      I hope you do too! 🕸
